sections.b:
Joseph is seventeen when the story begins: his father's favorite, dressed in a long robe, dreaming that his family will bow to him (37:2–11). His brothers sell him to traders bound for Egypt (37:28). As a slave in Potiphar's house he rises to manager, refuses his master's wife, and is jailed on her false charge (39). In prison he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker (40), and two years later Pharaoh's own dreams of fat and thin cows (41). At thirty he becomes Pharaoh's second in command, marries Asenath and stores grain for the famine.

When his brothers come to buy grain, he recognizes them, tests them, and finally reveals himself: "I am Joseph... God sent me here before you to keep people alive" (45:3–5). He brings his father's family to Goshen, manages Egypt through the famine (47), receives a double portion through his sons Ephraim and Manasseh (48), and after Jacob's death reassures his brothers: "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (50:20). He dies at 110, making Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan (50:24–26).

sections.h: Joseph as a type of Christ
sections.b: From the second century on, Christian writers (Tertullian, Ambrose, Augustine and many others) read Joseph as a type of Christ: the beloved son sent to his brothers, hated and sold for silver, stripped of his robe, falsely accused and counted among criminals, raised from the "pit" to the king's right hand at about thirty, given a new name, providing bread for the world, forgiving those who wronged him, and saving "many people" through their evil (50:20; Acts 2:23). The New Testament itself never calls Joseph a type, though Stephen's speech draws the parallel of a deliverer first rejected by his brothers (Acts 7:9–14, 35). Many modern interpreters accept the broad pattern while warning against pressing every detail.

Jewish tradition calls him Yosef ha-tsaddiq, "Joseph the righteous," chiefly for refusing Potiphar's wife (39:9). The rabbis also criticize the young Joseph for vanity and tale-bearing, and debate his harshness toward his brothers. Joseph became the model of a Jew who serves a foreign ruler faithfully without losing his identity, a pattern echoed in Daniel, Esther and Mordecai. Later works retold his life: Joseph and Aseneth, the Testament of Joseph, and the Midrash, which imagines his father's face stopping him from sin (Talmud, Sotah 36b). The Qur'an devotes a whole chapter, Surah 12, to Yusuf.

Most critical scholars read Genesis 37–50 as a novella, a carefully crafted short story, rather than a chronicle; Gerhard von Rad linked it to Israel's wisdom tradition, and Donald Redford dated it to the 600s–400s BC on the basis of its Egyptian names and customs. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier argue that its Egyptian details (slave prices, titles, loanwords, investiture, embalming, the 110-year life span) fit the second millennium BC. Egyptology has found no record of Joseph himself; it shows that the setting is realistic but cannot prove or disprove the events.

The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) speaks of a Messiah son of Joseph who will be killed, beside the Messiah son of David who will reign, and applies to him the mourning of Zechariah 12:10. The figure draws on Joseph's suffering and rise and on the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, whose rivalry with Judah runs through the Bible (Psalm 78:67–68; Ezekiel 37:15–28). Christian scholars often discuss it beside the New Testament's single Messiah who suffers and then reigns.

common: Joseph had a "coat of many colors" (the Hebrew probably means a long robe with sleeves; see 37:3).
Joseph's brothers sold him directly to Egypt (the text names two groups of traders, and readers still debate who sold him).
uncommon: Some modern readers think Joseph's harsh treatment of his brothers in chapters 42–44 was revenge rather than a test.
Joseph's land policy in 47:13–26 has been read as the beginning of the state slavery Israel later suffered (Leon Kass, Aaron Wildavsky).

claude.title: The dreamer who stops dreaming
claude.body: My own observation: Joseph dreams only as a teenager (37:5–9). After that he never dreams again; he interprets other people's dreams, and only once "remembers" his own (42:9). I think the story is tracing a change from a young man who sees himself at the center of the world to a man who sees himself as a servant of a larger plan: "It is not in me" (41:16), "God sent me" (45:5), "Am I in God's place?" (50:19). The dreams come true precisely when he stops trying to make them come true.

sections.b: Judah first appears in Joseph's story as the brother who says "What is the profit if we kill our brother?" and proposes selling him instead (37:26–27). In chapter 38 he leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite, fails his daughter-in-law Tamar, and is confronted with his own seal and staff, confessing, "She is more in the right than I am" (38:26). From chapter 43 on he becomes the family's leader: he pledges himself for Benjamin (43:8–10), confesses the brothers' guilt (44:16), and offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:18–34). Jacob sends him ahead to Goshen (46:28) and gives him the scepter: "Judah, your brothers will praise you... The scepter will not leave Judah" (49:8–12).

Judah's story is one of the Bible's clearest portraits of moral change. The man who sold one son of Rachel offers himself for the other; the father who sent away his son's widow speaks with tenderness of his own father's grief. Jewish commentators often use Maimonides' definition of complete repentance, refusing the same sin in the same situation, to describe Judah, and Genesis Rabbah (99:8) and the Tosefta (Berakhot 4:18) connect his tribe's kingship with his public confession. Christian readers see in Judah's offer a picture of substitution fulfilled by Jesus, "descended from Judah" (Hebrews 7:14).

common: All of Joseph's brothers were equally guilty (the text sets apart Reuben, who tried to rescue him, and Judah, who proposed selling him instead of killing him).
uncommon: Some critical scholars think Genesis 38 and Judah's speeches were shaped in Judah to justify the rule of David's tribe over Joseph's northern tribes.
Following Rashbam on 37:28, a few interpreters hold that Midianites pulled Joseph from the pit before Judah's sale could happen, so that the brothers never sold him themselves.

claude.title: Two pledges
claude.body: My own observation, building on the link between the Hebrew words: Judah gives a pledge twice. In 38:17–18 he gives Tamar his seal, cord and staff as an 'eravon, a pledge, for a night's pleasure. In 43:9 he becomes the 'arev, the guarantor, for Benjamin, pledging himself. The first pledge exposed him; the second redeemed him. The story measures Judah's growth by what he is willing to put on the line.

sections.b: Tamar marries Er, Judah's firstborn, who dies; his brother Onan refuses to give her a child and dies too. Judah sends her home "until my son Shelah is grown" but never gives her to him (38:6–14). She disguises herself by the road to Timnah, conceives by Judah, and keeps his seal, cord and staff. When she is condemned to be burned, she sends them to him privately: "Please look closely. Whose are these?" Judah confesses, "She is more in the right than I am" (38:25–26). Her twins Perez and Zerah are born, and Perez becomes the ancestor of Boaz and David.

The Talmud praises her for refusing to shame Judah in public, even at the risk of death (Sotah 10b). Feminist interpreters see a woman left powerless by the men of her family who acts boldly to claim her rights. Christian readers note that Matthew names her first of four women in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:3, 5, 6), each with an irregular story, as a sign of grace. Older scholarship called the "holy woman" of 38:21 a temple prostitute, but this is now widely doubted (Westenholz).

uncommon: Tamar is never called a prostitute by the narrator except through Judah's eyes and the townspeople's rumor (38:15, 24).

sections.b: Genesis 38 is the Bible's earliest example of brother-in-law marriage. Judah tells his second son, "Do a brother-in-law's duty to her, and raise up offspring for your brother" (38:8). Onan's refusal, using Tamar while ensuring no child would be born, is condemned (38:9–10). When Judah withholds his third son, Tamar secures the child through Judah himself, and Judah admits she was in the right. Hittite law 193 allowed the duty to pass to the father-in-law when no brother was available, which may explain why the outcome is treated as legitimate. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 later regulates the custom, and Ruth 4:12 recalls Tamar's son Perez.

common: Onan's sin was masturbation (the text condemns his refusal to give his brother an heir).

sections.h: "God sent me": providence in the Joseph story
sections.b: God speaks openly only once in Genesis 37–50 (46:2–4) and works no miracles. Yet the story is the Bible's great narrative of providence. A stranger in a field points Joseph to his brothers (37:15–17), a caravan passes at the right moment (37:25), a cupbearer forgets and then remembers (40:23; 41:9). Joseph himself draws the conclusion twice: "God sent me here before you to keep people alive" (45:5–8), and "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (50:20). The brothers' guilt is not erased, but God's purpose is greater than their plan. Psalm 105:17 sums it up: "He had sent someone on before them; / Joseph was sold off to be a slave."

Christian theology has used 50:20 to explain how God can be sovereign over evil acts without being their author, especially at the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Jewish thought holds a similar balance: "All is foreseen, yet freedom is given" (Mishnah Avot 3:15). Some modern readers prefer to say that God brings good out of evil rather than intending the events themselves. The verb in 50:20 is the same for both: the brothers "planned" and God "planned."

uncommon: The Joseph story mentions God's direct speech only once, in a night vision to Jacob (46:2–4).

sections.b: Genesis 49:28 is the first time the Bible counts "the tribes of Israel, twelve of them." Jacob's poem gives each son a saying that later Israel read as the destiny of his tribe: Reuben loses first place, Simeon and Levi are scattered, Judah receives the scepter, Zebulun lives by the sea, Issachar labors, Dan judges and strikes like a snake, Gad raids, Asher grows rich food, Naphtali runs free, Joseph is fruitful and blessed, Benjamin is a wolf. Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 is a parallel poem. Most scholars think the sayings were collected in the time of the judges or early kings.

Jacob adopts Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own (48:5), so Joseph becomes two tribes. When Levi becomes the priestly tribe without land, the territorial tribes still number twelve (Joshua 14:3–4). Lists vary: Revelation 7:5–8 includes Joseph and Manasseh, leaves out Dan and Ephraim, and has Levi, a puzzle discussed since Irenaeus.

uncommon: Some scholars think the twelve-tribe system is an idealized scheme drawn up later, not the original shape of early Israel.

sections.b: Genesis 37–50 is full of Egyptian color: the Nile (ye'or, an Egyptian word) and its reeds, magicians who are lector priests, Pharaoh's signet ring, linen and gold collar, the priest of On (Heliopolis), Egyptian names (Potiphar, Asenath, Zaphenath-paneah), embalming, seventy days of mourning, and a perfect life of 110 years. Egyptologists agree that these details fit Egypt; they disagree about which period they fit best. Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier argue for the second millennium BC; Donald Redford argued that many details fit best in the 600s–400s BC. No Egyptian record mentions Joseph.

In Joseph's day Egypt is the place of survival: "God sent me here before you to keep people alive" (45:5). God promises Jacob, "I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again" (46:4). But even in Genesis there are warning signs: Egyptians despise shepherds (46:34), the people sell themselves to Pharaoh (47:19–25), and Jacob and Joseph insist on burial in Canaan (47:29–30; 50:25). Exodus 1:8 begins with a Pharaoh "who did not know Joseph."

common: The Bible's Egypt stories are contradicted by archaeology (in fact the Joseph setting is realistic, though Joseph himself is unattested).

sections.b: The Joseph story turns on three pairs of dreams. Joseph dreams of sheaves and of stars bowing to him (37:5–11); the cupbearer and baker dream of a vine and of baskets (40:5–19); Pharaoh dreams of cows and of grain (41:1–7). Joseph explains the rule: a doubled dream means God has firmly decided (41:32). Unlike Egypt's professional dream readers, who had written manuals such as the Chester Beatty Dream Book, Joseph insists that "interpretations belong to God" (40:8; 41:16). His own dreams come true when the brothers bow to the ground (42:6; 43:26; 50:18).

uncommon: Some readers think Joseph's own dreams were youthful ambition rather than revelation, since God is never said to send them.

sections.h: Shiloh and the scepter of Judah
sections.b: "The scepter will not leave Judah... until Shiloh comes, and to him the peoples will give obedience" (Genesis 49:10) is one of the oldest texts read as messianic. All three Aramaic Targums render it "until the Messiah comes," the Talmud lists Shiloh among the Messiah's names (Sanhedrin 98b), and a Dead Sea Scrolls commentary (4Q252) speaks of "the Messiah of righteousness, the branch of David." Christian writers from Justin Martyr argued that the scepter passed from Judah when Herod ruled and Jesus was born. Jewish teachers answered that the scepter had not departed: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 5a) finds it in the exilarchs of Babylon and in Hillel's descendants, and Nachmanides argued at Barcelona (1263) that Judah's kingship had lapsed long before, in 586 BC, so the verse cannot fix the date of the Messiah. Many modern scholars read the verse as originally a promise about David's dynasty. The meaning of "Shiloh" itself is uncertain (see the variant on 49:10).

Jacob's picture of Judah's king tying "his donkey's colt to the choice vine" (49:11) is echoed in Zechariah 9:9's humble king "riding on a donkey, on a colt," which the Gospels apply to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2–7; John 12:14–15). The robe washed in "the blood of grapes" recurs in the divine warrior of Isaiah 63:1–3 and Revelation 19:13.

uncommon: Some Christian readers have noted that the word for "rescue" in 49:18, yeshu'ah, is close to the Hebrew name of Jesus, Yeshua.

sections.b: Long before David, Jacob says to Judah, "The scepter will not leave Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet" (Genesis 49:10). Most readers, ancient and modern, see the promise fulfilled first in David, the shepherd of Bethlehem in Judah, and his royal line (2 Samuel 7:12–16). David's ancestry runs through Judah's son Perez, born to Tamar (Genesis 38:29; Ruth 4:18–22), and 1 Chronicles 5:2 explains that "Judah prevailed over his brothers, and from him came a ruler."

The personal name YHWH ("the LORD") is rare in the Joseph story: the narrator uses it in chapters 38–39 (eight times in chapter 39, framing Joseph's slavery and prison with "the LORD was with Joseph") and Jacob once in prayer (49:18). Elsewhere characters say "God" (Elohim), especially when speaking to Egyptians. Jacob calls on El Shaddai, "God Almighty" (43:14; 48:3), and in his last words piles up titles: "the God of your father," "the Almighty," "the Mighty One of Jacob," "the Shepherd," "the Stone of Israel" (49:24–25), and "the angel who has redeemed me" (48:16). Jacob is the first in the Bible to call God his shepherd (48:15).

The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27, Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 says seventy of Jacob's family went down to Egypt. The Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy-five, adding five descendants of Joseph in Genesis 46:20, and two Dead Sea Scrolls (4QExod-b and 4QGen-Exod-a) seem to read seventy-five at Exodus 1:5, though the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 10:22 says seventy. No Qumran copy of Genesis 46:27 itself is known. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:14 follows the Greek. Other places in Genesis 37–50 where the Greek or Samaritan text differs include 47:21 ("made them slaves"), 47:31 ("staff" instead of "bed," quoted in Hebrews 11:21) 49:10 ("until the things stored up for him come"), the redivided letters of 49:19–20, and 37:28, where the Greek price is twenty pieces of gold.

sections.h: Down to Egypt, and the promise of coming up
sections.b: The end of Genesis sets up the exodus. God promises Jacob at Beersheba, "I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again" (46:4). Seventy people go down (46:27); they are "fruitful and multiplied greatly" (47:27; Exodus 1:7). Jacob's funeral procession brings his family to Canaan and back, escorted by Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen (50:7–9), a peaceful preview of a very different journey. Joseph's dying words, "God will surely come to help you" (paqod yifqod), become the words Moses brings (Exodus 3:16), and his bones go up with Israel (50:25; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32).

sections.h: The seventy who went to Egypt
sections.b: Genesis 46:8–27 lists the sons and grandsons of Jacob who went down to Egypt, arranged by mother: Leah's line (33, counting Jacob or, in rabbinic tradition, Jochebed), Zilpah's (16), Rachel's (14) and Bilhah's (7), for seventy in all. Exodus 1:1 opens with the same words, "These are the names," and Numbers 26 gives the later clans of the same families. The list includes some who seem too young to have children yet (Perez's sons, Benjamin's ten), which suggests it records the founding clans of Israel rather than a head count on one day.

Genesis 42–50 is the Bible's first long story of repentance and reconciliation. The brothers name their sin unprompted: "Truly we are guilty over our brother" (42:21). They accept guilt together (44:16). Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33), showing change in action. Joseph forgives (45:4–15) and reassures them again when they fear revenge after Jacob's death (50:15–21). Maimonides defined complete repentance as refusing the same sin in the same situation (Laws of Repentance 2:1), and Jewish commentators apply this to Judah.

uncommon: Some readers doubt that Jacob ever gave the message the brothers report in 50:16–17; the rabbis themselves thought it was invented for the sake of peace (Talmud, Yevamot 65b).

sections.b: The verb ga'al, "to redeem" as a family rescuer, appears for the first time in the Bible in Jacob's blessing: "the angel who has redeemed me from all harm" (Genesis 48:16). Jacob uses the language of family rescue for God's protection through his long life. Jewish tradition made the verse a children's bedtime prayer (Hamalakh hago'el); many church fathers identified the angel with the Son of God.

The Joseph story is one of the richest sources of Christian typology. Joseph, the beloved son, rejected, sold for silver, falsely accused, raised to the right hand of the king and forgiving his brothers, was read from the early church on as a type of Christ. Other details drew typological readings: Judah's pledge for Benjamin (43:9; Hebrews 7:22), Jacob's crossed hands as a sign of the cross (48:14, Tertullian), and the donkey's colt of 49:11 (Matthew 21:2–7). The New Testament does not call Joseph a type, though Stephen draws the parallel (Acts 7:9–14). Jewish readers object that such readings can turn Joseph into a mere preview of someone else; Jewish tradition reads the fathers' lives as signs for Israel's own later history instead.

The first time Sheol is named in the Bible, Jacob is mourning Joseph: "I will go down to my son in Sheol, still mourning" (Genesis 37:35). He uses the word three more times, always of his own death in grief (42:38; 44:29, 31). For Jacob, Sheol is not a place of punishment but the common destination of the dead, where he expects to join his son.

Judah marries a Canaanite (38:2), and Simeon's son Shaul is born to a Canaanite woman (46:10). Joseph marries Asenath, daughter of an Egyptian priest (41:45), whose sons become two tribes of Israel. Jacob's family lives in Egypt as resident foreigners (47:4), a memory Israel's law later uses: "you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 23:9). Later Jewish writers were uneasy with Asenath and told of her conversion (Joseph and Aseneth) or made her Dinah's daughter (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan).

In Genesis 37–50 Jacob is a grieving father who refuses comfort for Joseph (37:35) and clings to Benjamin (42:38), until he lets go: "If I am bereaved, I am bereaved" (43:14). Told that Joseph lives, his spirit revives (45:27). God speaks to him one last time at Beersheba (46:2–4). He blesses Pharaoh, sums up his years of wandering as "few and full of trouble" (47:9), adopts Ephraim and Manasseh, crossing his hands to put the younger first (48), and speaks the poem of the twelve tribes (49). He dies at 147, is embalmed in Egypt, and is buried at Machpelah (50:1–13). Hebrews 11:21 counts his blessing of Joseph's sons as faith.

uncommon: The rabbis noted that Genesis never says Jacob "died" (49:33), and Rabbi Yohanan taught, "Jacob our father did not die" (Talmud, Ta'anit 5b).

sections.b: Jacob, who took his father's blessing by deception (27), ends his life by giving blessings with open eyes, though nearly blind. He blesses Pharaoh twice (47:7, 10). He blesses Joseph's sons, deliberately putting the younger Ephraim first (48:14–20), as Isaac had unknowingly blessed the younger Jacob. In chapter 49 he speaks to each son "the blessing that was his" (49:28), some of them more rebukes than blessings. Reuben loses the firstborn's place; the birthright passes to Joseph's sons and the leadership to Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1–2).

When Jacob crosses his hands to bless Joseph's younger son first, he says, "I know, my son, I know" (48:19). The pattern of the younger chosen over the elder runs through Genesis: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Perez (38:29), Joseph and Ephraim. Paul uses it to argue that God's choice depends on his call, not on birth order or merit (Romans 9:10–13).

Rachel is dead before Genesis 37 begins, but her presence fills the Joseph story. Her two sons are the father's favorites (37:3; 44:20, 27). On his deathbed Jacob remembers burying her "on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)" (48:7), just as he adopts Joseph's sons, perhaps giving her the sons she did not live to bear. Rashi says Jacob explains why she was not buried at Machpelah: so that she could weep for her children as they went into exile (Jeremiah 31:15).

Joseph's brothers take the flock to Shechem, where Jacob's family had a violent history (37:12–14; 34). Jacob gives Joseph "one shoulder" (shekhem) of land, a pun on the city's name (48:22), and Joseph's bones are later buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob bought (Joshua 24:32; John 4:5).

sections.h: Leah in the tomb of the fathers
sections.b: Genesis never reports Leah's death; we learn only from Jacob's last words that he buried her in the cave of Machpelah (49:31), where he too will lie. Rachel, the beloved wife, lies alone by the road to Bethlehem (48:7). Leah's sons Levi and Judah become the tribes of priests and kings.

sections.h: Rachel's grave on the road to Bethlehem
sections.b: Jacob recalls burying Rachel "on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)" (Genesis 48:7; compare 35:19). The traditional Rachel's Tomb stands at the northern entrance to Bethlehem. Matthew links Rachel's weeping (Jeremiah 31:15) to the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).
